articles.content_excerpt: Lula vs. Bolsonaro in Brazil's Presidential Election Authors Black Agenda Radio with Margaret Kimberley bareditors Fri, 10/09/2026 - 05:05 Brazil's incumbent president Lula da Silva finished second behind Flavio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential election. Because neither man received at least 51% of the vote, a run-off election on October 25 will decide the presidency. articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: Given all the headlines about the US government trying to deport one or another migrant over their foreign policy views, you’d be forgiven for thinking this is a uniquely Trumpian innovation. Sadly, as the recent developments out of Latvia show, it’s far from it. Yesterday news broke that Leonid Ragozin, an exiled Russian journalist who has lived in the Baltic country for over a decade (and is also a Jacobin contributor who I interviewed for a forthcoming piece) has been declared persona non grata by the Latvian government, which intends to swiftly deport him. articles.title: Local 115 Wins Wage Increases, Firm Limits on Mandatory Overtime in Second UE Pact
articles.content_excerpt: The members of UE Local 115 ratified a new three-year agreement on August 27 after four months of negotiations. Refresco employees bottle beverage products like Gatorade, Bodyarmor, Tropicana, and generic sodas for various supermarket chains. The contract, Local 115’s second with Refresco, includes an average 14 percent wage increase across the life of the agreement, establishes firm limits on mandatory overtime, and lowers penalties for attendance infractions. Members making less than $24.00 an hour are set to receive general wage increases of 5.5, 4.25, and 4 percent in each year respectively, with all other workers receiving 4, 3.25, and 3 percent increases. articles.title: Local 221 Ratifies Contract Amidst Federal Cuts
articles.content_excerpt: At the end of September, UE Local 221 members who work for the Head Start program at Northeast Kingdom Community Action (NEKCA) ratified a two-year contract that includes wage increases and improvements to language. The benefits in the contract were won despite $1.2 million of federal funding cut to the Head Start program. The members won a $250 one-time stipend for full-time employees and a $100 stipend for part-time employees. The contract includes a 1.5 percent wage increase and the option for members to negotiate future cost-of-living adjustments during the life of the contract. The members also won layoff protections — extending the layoff recall list from 12 to 18 months for employees with one to three years of service. articles.title: More Legal Cannabis
articles.author: Paul Armentano
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Most Americans now live in a jurisdiction where cannabis is legal — and use by teens has never been lower. Yes, you read that right. According to the latest findings from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, fewer young people nationwide are using marijuana today than at any time in the last 30 years. In the 24 states where adult-use cannabis markets are legally regulated, teen use has plummeted . For example, cannabis use by high schoolers fell over 60 percent in Colorado following legalization. articles.title: AI Ripoff Economy
articles.author: Lindsay Owens
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Every day, companies find better, and sneakier, ways to reach deeper into our wallets. They trap us in subscriptions, bury fees until checkout, use algorithms to collude with competitors, and mine our personal data to charge us the most we’re willing to pay. With each trick and tactic, companies are reinventing the ripoff right under our noses. And, as families strain under the rising cost of living, these practices are coming for every line of the household budget. Algorithmic price fixing is one of the most powerful tools in that arsenal. articles.title: Where Are the Democratic Socialists of America Going?
articles.author: Paul Heideman
articles.content_excerpt: The history of the American left is marked by imposing peaks and valleys. Over the last century and a half, organizations have sprung up and, often within a decade of their founding, become major institutions of US politics. They have typically declined nearly as quickly, with few sustaining their positions in American society longer than a decade or so. The Populist Party emerged in the early 1890s, won nearly 10 percent of the vote in the 1892 presidential election, and had largely disappeared by 1900. The Communist Party, founded in 1919, reached about seventy-five thousand members in the mid-1940s, only to collapse, through repression and its own mistakes, to under ten thousand by the end of the 1950s. articles.title: Under Trump Pressure, Bolivia Arrests Its Own Attorney General
articles.author: Joseph Bouchard
articles.content_excerpt: Early last week, the Trump administration’s State Department announced visa restrictions on a group of Latin American officials it accused of corruption and of “undermining democratically-selected governments.” Of the twenty-one people it targeted in Bolivia, Washington chose to name only one: Bolivia’s sitting attorney general, Roger Mariaca. A little over twenty-four hours later, on September 30, Bolivian police detained Mariaca at Viru Viru International Airport in Santa Cruz while agents raided prosecutors’ offices in Sucre and Santa Cruz. Craig Unit 1, a coal-fired power plant distinguished by tall exhaust smokestacks that rise above a rolling landscape in northwestern Colorado, was scheduled to close for good at the end of 2025 amid pressure from environmental advocates, public interest groups and state officials. But on Dec. 30, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to keep burning coal. The unit had suffered a mechanical failure 11 days earlier and was not even running. Wright has since renewed the order three times — most recently on Sept. 25, extending the plant’s life through Christmas Day, a full year past its retirement date. articles.title: Marx Believed Meaningful Work Was Central to the Good Life
articles.author: Jan Kandiyali
articles.content_excerpt: Not too long ago, a wave of books written by left-wing and liberal commentators appeared celebrating a future in which work would be a thing of the past. The increased productivity of technology would free humans from drudgery and allow them to focus on cultural pursuits and spend more time making friends or finding love, these polemics alleged. Amid the near-daily stream of stories warning about the disastrous social effects that artificial intelligence may have, not just on the labor market but on people’s literacy and numeracy, this earlier mood seems at best misguided.
